title: Growing garlic
subtitle: Autumn planting for a summer harvest, with hardneck and softneck varieties
excerpt: Garlic is planted in October or November in the UK as individual cloves and harvested the following June or July. It needs a cold period to develop a full bulb; autumn planting outdoors provides this naturally.
sourceNotes: RHS garlic growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA agricultural extension notes on allium production, public domain. Mrs Earle, Pot-Pourri from a Surrey Garden (1897), Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: Garlic varieties that produce a stiff central stem (scape) in late spring. Hardneck types have fewer, larger cloves than softneck and a stronger, more complex flavour. They store for three to five months after harvest. UK-suited hardneck varieties include Chesnok Red, Mersley White, and Purple Wight.

Garlic varieties without a central flowering stem, with a flexible dried neck that can be plaited. Softneck types produce more cloves per bulb and store longer (six to nine months) than hardneck types. Varieties include Picardy Wight and Cristo. Most supermarket garlic is softneck.

content.text: Garlic is planted as individual cloves in October or November and harvested the following June or July. It needs a cold period of six to eight weeks below 10°C to develop a full multi-clove bulb; autumn planting outdoors provides this.

Full sun, well-drained soil. Garlic does poorly in waterlogged ground, particularly over winter; bulbs rot in standing water. Raised beds or a well-drained border suit it well. Rotate garlic around the plot with onions, leeks, and shallots; do not grow alliums in the same spot for more than two years running.

Buy certified disease-free seed garlic from a reputable supplier; supermarket garlic is treated to prevent sprouting and usually fails. Separate the bulb into individual cloves and plant the largest, healthiest ones. Plant cloves 5 cm deep (tip upward), 15 cm apart, in rows 30 cm apart. Plant in October; November is still acceptable in the south but later than that risks incomplete vernalisation.

The plants overwinter as short green shoots. Growth accelerates in late March and April. On hardneck varieties, a curling flower stem (scape) appears in May; cut this off at the base as soon as you see it. Leaving the scape reduces the bulb size. The scapes are edible: mild-flavoured, they are good chopped into scrambled eggs or stir-fried.
Stop watering (if you have been watering at all) in late May as the bulbs ripen. Feeding is not necessary if the soil is reasonably fertile.

Harvest when the lower leaves have yellowed and the remaining foliage is still green. This is usually late June or early July. If all the leaves die back, the bulbs will have started to separate into individual cloves and will store less well. Lift carefully with a fork; garlic skins bruise easily. Leave on the surface for a few days to dry in a warm, airy place before tying or plaiting for storage.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: What goes wrong most often with garlic.

items.symptom: Bulbs are small and unsplit (single round 'rounds')
items.cause: Insufficient cold period, planted in spring rather than autumn.
items.fix: Always plant in autumn for UK conditions. Spring-planted garlic in the UK rarely develops a proper multi-clove bulb.
Improve drainage before the next planting. Raise the bed by 10 cm if the site holds water. Plant into sharp sand at the base of each planting hole if drainage is marginal.
Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation by increasing spacing. Rust rarely kills garlic; the bulbs are usually sound at harvest.
